title: Built-in types (numbers, text, and bool)
hook: C# gives you a menu of ready-made types for whole numbers, decimals, true/false, single characters, and text. Pick the right number type on purpose — money and grades need `decimal`, not `double`.

blocks.text: **Built-in types** are the primitive types the language and runtime provide out of the box. You do not declare them — you use them directly: `int` for whole numbers, `double` for approximate floating-point math, `decimal` for base-10 fractions (money, grade point averages), `bool` for true/false, `char` for a single character, and `string` for text. Most built-in numerics and `bool` are **value types** (they copy on assignment). `string` is a **reference type** even though it behaves like an immutable value in many ways.

entries.plainDefinition: A whole number from about −2 billion to +2 billion. The default choice for counters, indexes, and IDs that fit.
A number type designed for base-10 math. Use it for currency, grades, and anything you print as dollars or a report card.
entries.example: `decimal fee = 19.99m;` — note the `m` suffix on the literal.

entries.plainDefinition: Fast approximate math like JavaScript's `number`. Good for graphics transforms and science; bad for money.
entries.example: `double scale = 1.5;` for a SkiaSharp zoom factor.

entries.plainDefinition: A sequence of characters stored as an immutable reference type. Once created, its content cannot change — you create a new string instead.

blocks.text: Choosing the wrong numeric type causes real bugs. `0.1 + 0.2` with `double` does not equal `0.3` — the same family of rounding error as JavaScript `number`. A CSV grade importer that parses `3.50` into `double` and then rounds can produce `3.499999999`. Use `decimal` for anything financial or academic. Use `double` for pixel coordinates and physics. `bool` is not an integer in C# (unlike C) — you cannot silently add `true + 1`.

blocks.title: Quick picker
blocks.body: Counters and array indexes → `int` or `long`. Money, fees, GPA → `decimal` with the `m` suffix. SkiaSharp transforms, sensor readings → `double`. Text → `string`. Yes/no flags → `bool`.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

items.title: Ask: is it an exact whole number?
items.body: Use `int`, `long`, `byte`, or their unsigned variants (`uint`, `ulong`). No fractions, no rounding surprises.

items.title: Ask: is it money or a grade?
items.body: Use `decimal`. Append `m` to literals (`19.99m`). Accept the small performance cost for correct base-10 math.

items.title: Ask: is it a measurement or graphics value?
items.body: Use `double` (or `float` when memory matters). Expect binary floating-point imprecision.

items.title: Remember: string is special
items.body: `string` is a reference type but compares by content with `==`. It is immutable — concatenation creates new objects.

snippet.label: decimal for grades and money
snippet.explanation: Line 1–2: the `m` suffix marks a `decimal` literal. Line 5: `double` is correct for graphics scaling where tiny imprecision is acceptable. Line 6: `int` for a whole-number cap. Interview answer: `decimal` for anything you would print as currency or a report card.

snippet.label: double imprecision vs decimal exactness
snippet.explanation: Lines 1–2: binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 exactly — same surprise as JavaScript. Lines 4–5: `decimal` stores base-10 fractions correctly. Line 8: C# does not treat `bool` as `0`/`1` like C does.

snippet.label: Parsing CSV scores into the right type
snippet.code:
string raw = "3.50";

decimal grade = decimal.Parse(raw);   // correct for GPA
double approx = double.Parse(raw);    // risky for reports

char letter = 'A';                    // single UTF-16 code unit
string fullName = "Ada Lovelace";     // immutable text
snippet.explanation: Line 3: parse grades into `decimal` so `3.50` stays `3.50`. Line 4: `double.Parse` works but introduces binary rounding. Line 6: `char` holds one character; full names belong in `string`. `char` is not a full Unicode emoji — surrogate pairs need `string` or `Rune`.

blocks.title: Numbers across languages
rows: No decimal primitive — use a library or integer cents

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Using `float` or `double` for money because JSON numbers look like floats. Parsing CSV scores into `double` then rounding in surprising ways. Assuming `char` is a full Unicode character — emoji and some scripts need two `char` values (a surrogate pair) inside a `string`.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: decimal uses 128 bits with base-10 semantics — GPA and fee calculations stay exact where double drifts like JavaScript number. In Redis cache TTL math, prefer long seconds with explicit bounds over double. char is UTF-16 code units, not full graphemes — user-visible length belongs on string with StringInfo, not raw char count. bool does not implicitly convert to int — unlike C, which prevents if (flags) style bugs at compile time.

blocks.title: Tradeoffs at senior level
rows: Slower than double — acceptable for correctness
Not one user-perceived character for emoji

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Using double for money without mentioning decimal. Saying string is a value type because == compares content. Treating char as a full Unicode character for emoji. Claiming bool converts to int like C.

interviewTakeaways: decimal for money and grades; double for graphics and measurements.
string is a reference type; int and decimal are value types.
char is UTF-16 code unit — emoji may need two char values in a string.
60s: decimal for money. double for SkiaSharp. string is reference. bool is not int.

jsTsCorrelations.note: JavaScript `number` is always a double. `bigint` handles large integers only. C# splits `int`/`long`/`double`/`decimal` as separate first-class types you pick at compile time.
